newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Mexico blocks Western move on land mines ban.
newsitem.headline: Mexico blocks Western move on land mines ban.

text.p: Mexico, which says it has no anti-personnel mines of its own, blocked an attempt by Western countries at the Conference on Disarmament on Thursday to start negotiations on clinching a global ban on land mines.
Western diplomats in Geneva expressed confusion and disappointment over the veto, saying it seemed to break a Mexican government pledge won by U.S. President Clinton last month.
They said prospects now appeared dimmer for a breakthrough during the current session ending on June 27 and probably even at the final seven-week round starting in late July.
The 61-member forum, sponsored by the United Nations, has been trying to adopt its 1997 work programme since January but has been paralysed by a split over its priorities.
In a tactical manoeuvre, Western countries keen to start work on a ban on land mines tried to bring any objectors out into the open.
Finland, supported by Australia, Britain, France and the United States, called on members opposed to appointing a special coordinator on land mines to declare so publicly.
The request was designed to embarrass non-aligned states accused of behind-the-scenes moves to obstruct progress.
After three hours of heated debate, Mexican ambassador Antonio de Icaza objected to the conference president putting the Finnish question and thereby blocked the necessary consensus decision.

He said Mexico did not regard the Geneva forum as the appropriate one for land mines negotiations. His country could be flexible, he said, but such an appointment should be made in the context of a wider disarmament package proposed by non-aligned states.
Absa Claude Diallo, Senegal's ambassador who now presides over the forum, said: "We have a clear position. There is no consensus on the request for appointment of a special coordinator on mines."
"Mexico blocked it. Clearly Mexico wants to be seen as a champion of nuclear disarmament and also keep mines for possible use in Chiapas," said one Western diplomat.

"The decision was blocked by one delegation -- Mexico. We have our answer now," said another Western diplomat. "During the debate, Cuba and Syria obviously shared Mexico's view, but didn't feel the need to stand up and be counted."
In Mexico City, Foreign Minister Jose Angel Gurria denied that Mexico was using land mines in Chiapas, a southern state which saw an Indian uprising in 1994 and is still a trouble-spot.

"In Mexico, there are no mines and we don't produce mines. We don't have a land mines industry and mines are not used for any purpose and will never be used, " he told Reuters in a telephone interview, adding that Mexico was "a champion of a total land mine ban."

He said the Mexican position in Geneva was based on a fear that the process of getting a ban in the Conference on Disarmament would be very long and very slow. Mexico wanted to give priority to a parallel forum called the "Ottawa process".
The acting head of the U.S. delegation, Katherine Crittenberger, urged all members of the conference to state their positions openly. "We would like to know where we stand," she said bluntly.

Under the Finnish proposal, the special coordinatror would have been asked to seek consensus on a mandate for launching negotiations on a ban on land mines, which are blamed for killing 25,000 people a year and maiming many more.
Western states are keen to launch such talks in the Geneva body in parallel to Canada's "Ottawa Process," which aims to reach a ban among some 50 countries by the end of the year.

But China and Russia, major producers and users of land mines, are not taking a formal part in the Canadian-sponsored forum. Western diplomats say this means a viable, universal ban can only be reached in Geneva.
But non-aligned countries say top priority should be given to concrete steps towards total nuclear disarmament and only then would they be ready to work on issues including land mines.
Mexico's de Icaza, on behalf of a group of non-aligned countries, introduced the text of a mandate for a new committee to negotiate total nuclear disarmament within a specified time.
The five declared nuclear nations -- the United States, Russia, China, France and Britain -- have refused to enter such discussions at this stage.
